prompt:
Output exactly one literal, factual sentence (8–20 words) describing only visible content in the image. Do not add labels, examples, lists, annotations, or any extra text.

Definitions: content words exclude a single leading article (a/an/the) and punctuation. A high‑signal token is one of: visible color or pattern, a concrete object class (prefer the most specific multiword class available, e.g., "electric guitar", "motorbike"), a clear count (Arabic numeral), clothing/accessory, or legible text/logo copied verbatim.

Primary rules:
- Include at least two high‑signal tokens within the first four content words when two are clearly visible; otherwise include at least one high‑signal token within the first three content words.
- If a visible color/pattern exists, place it immediately before its noun (e.g., "red bicycle"). Use "noun with [attribute]" only if the color cannot appear within the required early content words.
- Prefer the most specific visible concrete class; do not use generic nouns like "object", "instrument", or "item" when a specific class is clearly visible. Use "person" only when a more specific subject is not visually identifiable.
- If any legible text or logo is present and confidently readable, copy it exactly and place it within the first six content words.
- Use Arabic numerals for clear counts and place them early. Use "several" only for indistinct groups (>3).
- Allow either a short noun‑phrase caption (no verb) or a concise present‑tense sentence (present simple or present‑participle). If you use a verb, you may place it after the first four content words to keep high‑signal tokens early.
- Include at most one short spatial connector ("next to", "on", "near", "in front of") to link the primary subject to a nearby object or surface.
- Choose the primary subject deterministically: prefer the centermost, largest, highest‑contrast, or the object with an explicit visible attribute (color/number/logo).
- Do not infer unseen attributes (age, emotion, intent, relationships) and avoid figurative or subjective language. Do not invent specific attributes when they are not visually evident; fall back to a safe generic only if the specific class or attribute is not clearly visible.
- Count content words carefully (exclude the single leading article and punctuation) when locating the first N content words.
- Avoid leading generic templates like "A person..." or "There is..." when a more specific subject is visible.

Output exactly one short sentence only—no extra text.
